lessons.title: What Selling Equity Really Means: Ownership, Dilution and Control

children.text: "I still run this company. I own 40% of it, which is more than anyone else." Founders say versions of this sentence all the time, and they are usually half right. Ownership and control are related, but they are not the same thing, and selling equity affects both in ways that surprise people who have only ever thought about the headline valuation.

This lesson takes one fictional company through two funding rounds and shows exactly what moves: the share count, the percentages, the board, and the list of decisions the founder can no longer take alone.

body.text: Selling equity is not borrowing money against your company. It is permanently handing over a slice of everything the company will ever be worth, plus a say in how it is run.

children.text: What You Are Actually Selling
A company issues new shares to an investor. That sounds procedural. Here is what it actually transfers, permanently and with no repayment date.

cells: Every rupee of dividend the company ever declares is split with them, forever
If the company is sold or listed, they take their percentage of the proceeds
Their votes count at every shareholder meeting, in proportion to their holding
A voice in the room where decisions are actually made, which matters more than votes
Named decisions that cannot be taken without their written consent
Monthly or quarterly financials, budgets and access the company must provide

body.text: The last two lines are where founders are most often caught out. A 15% shareholder with a board seat and veto rights over the annual budget has far more influence than a 25% shareholder with neither. Read the shareholders' agreement, not just the percentage.

children.text: The Share Maths Nobody Explains

Meridian Learning is a fictional Hyderabad edtech company. Its two founders hold 10,00,000 equity shares between them, which is the whole company. An investor agrees to put in ₹6 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹15 crore.
The price per share comes from the pre-money valuation, not the post-money one. This is the step most people get wrong.

body.latex: \text{Price per share} = \frac{\text{Pre-money valuation}}{\text{Shares outstanding before the round}}
body.caption: The existing shareholders are being valued on what exists today

body.title: Find the price per share
body.prompt: Meridian Learning has 10,00,000 shares outstanding and is raising at a pre-money valuation of ₹15 crore. What price per share is the investor paying, in ₹?
body.explanation: ₹15,00,00,000 divided by 10,00,000 shares is ₹150 per share. Note that this uses the pre-money valuation, because those 10,00,000 shares are what exists before the new money arrives.

children.text: At ₹150 per share, ₹6 crore buys 4,00,000 new shares. The company issues them fresh, so the total rises from 10,00,000 to 14,00,000.

body.caption: Meridian Learning: before and after the angel round

body.text: The founders did not give away 4,00,000 of their own shares. They still hold exactly what they held before. Their stake fell because the denominator grew. This is the single most important mechanic in equity fundraising, and it repeats at every round.

body.title: Check the dilution
body.prompt: After the round, the founders hold 10,00,000 of 14,00,000 shares. What percentage of the company do they now own? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 10,00,000 divided by 14,00,000 is 71.43%, so about 71.4%. The angel holds the other 28.57%, which is ₹6 crore of a ₹21 crore post-money valuation.

body.title: The ESOP pool argument, and why it costs founders more than they expect

children.text: Almost every institutional investor asks the company to set aside an
ESOP pool
for employees, typically around 10% of the company. The fight is never about whether to have a pool. It is about when it is created.

markDefs.definition: Shares set aside to be granted to employees as stock options. It sits on the cap table and dilutes everyone else, whether or not the options have been granted yet.

children.text: If the pool is created after the round
, it dilutes everyone proportionally:
Founders: 71.43% becomes 64.29%
Angel: 28.57% becomes 25.71%
Pool: 10%
If the pool is carved out of the pre-money valuation
, which is what investors usually insist on, only the founders pay for it:
Founders: 61.43%
Angel: unchanged at 28.57%
Pool: 10%

Same headline valuation, same cheque, nearly 3 percentage points of difference to the founders. A term sheet that says "₹15 crore pre-money, including a 10% option pool" is quietly a lower valuation than one that says "₹15 crore pre-money, pool created post-round".
Round Two, and the 50% Line

Two years later Meridian Learning raises a Series A: ₹15 crore at a ₹60 crore pre-money valuation, giving the new investor 20% of the company. Everyone who was already on the cap table, including the pool, is diluted by the same fifth.

body.title: Meridian Learning ownership after the Series A (%)

children.text: The founders have gone from 100% to just over 49% in two rounds, without selling a single share of their own. Everything came from new shares being issued around them.

body.label: This is normal, not a failure
body.value: Infosys promoters held roughly 14% of the company in 2026
body.context: Founders of large Indian companies routinely end up with small minority stakes. Eternal, formerly Zomato, has no identified promoter group at all, and co-founder Deepinder Goyal held about 4.2% as of December 2024. Holdings change every quarter, so check the shareholding pattern on screener.in for the current figure before quoting any of these.

children.text: So Who Controls the Company Now?
Falling below 50% is a real event, but it does not automatically mean losing control. Voting power in an Indian company works in thresholds, set by the Companies Act, 2013.

stats.label: Pass a special resolution
stats.context: Changing the Articles, issuing shares to new investors

stats.label: Block a special resolution
stats.context: A negative control right that investors value highly

children.text: An
ordinary resolution
under Section 114(1) needs more votes for than against. A
special resolution

under Section 114(2) needs votes in favour of at least three times the votes against, which is why people describe it as a 75% threshold. Anyone holding more than 25% can therefore block a special resolution on their own, which is why investors negotiate so hard around that number.

markDefs.definition: A shareholder decision passed when votes in favour exceed votes against, under Section 114(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. Used for routine matters.
A shareholder decision needing votes in favour of at least three times the votes against, effectively 75% of votes cast, under Section 114(2) of the Companies Act, 2013.

body.text: At 49.14% the Meridian founders can no longer pass an ordinary resolution by themselves, but nobody else can either. Control now depends on who agrees with whom, on the composition of the board, and above all on the shareholders' agreement.

children.text: The Control That Does Not Show Up in Percentages
Two mechanisms shift real power regardless of shareholding. Both live in the shareholders' agreement rather than in the cap table.

columns.label: Board composition
points: The board takes most operating decisions, not the shareholders
Investors typically negotiate one seat per significant round
A founder-majority board can matter more than a founder-majority cap table
Watch for the right to appoint an observer, who attends but does not vote
Independent directors become mandatory as the company grows

columns.label: Reserved matters and veto rights
points: A list of decisions needing a named investor's consent
Typically: new share issues, new borrowing above a limit, selling the company
Also: changing the business, related party transactions, large capex, annual budget
A 15% holder with these rights can block far more than a 30% holder without them
They survive as long as the investor holds shares, unless the agreement says otherwise

children.text: These are commercial terms, not statutory ones, so they are negotiable at the term sheet stage. Term sheets are covered in depth by the dedicated course on this platform. What you need here is the instinct to look past the percentage.

body.title: The blocking number
body.textWithBlank: A shareholder holding more than ___ per cent of the votes can, on their own, block a special resolution.
body.explanation: A special resolution needs 75% of votes cast. Anything above 25% is therefore enough to stop one, which is why this threshold appears in so many Indian shareholder negotiations.

children.text: One More Thing the Company Must Do

Issuing shares is not just a transfer of money. Under Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company issuing new shares must follow a defined route: a rights issue to existing shareholders, an employee stock option scheme, or a preferential allotment to a specific investor, each with its own approvals. A preferential allotment needs shareholder approval by special resolution and a valuation report from a registered valuer.
If the new shares would exceed the
authorised share capital
in the Memorandum of Association, that limit has to be increased first. Rounds have been delayed by weeks because nobody checked this early enough.

markDefs.definition: The maximum amount of share capital a company is allowed to issue under its Memorandum of Association. It must be increased before issuing shares beyond it.

body.text: Company law procedure is summarised here to explain why fundraising takes time. It is not legal advice, and the exact approvals depend on the type of company and the structure of the round. Work with a company secretary or lawyer on any actual issue of shares.

body.title: What changed?
body.question: After Meridian Learning's angel round, the founders' stake fell from 100% to 71.43%. What happened to the number of shares the founders hold?
options: It depends on the price per share
body.explanation: The founders transferred nothing. The company created 4,00,000 brand new shares and sold them to the investor, so the denominator grew from 10,00,000 to 14,00,000. The founders still hold every share they held before.

body.title: Who has more power?
body.question: Investor A holds 30% with no board seat and no veto rights. Investor B holds 15%, has one of five board seats, and consent rights over new borrowing, the annual budget and any sale of the company. Who has more influence over day-to-day decisions?
options: Investor A, because percentage always decides
Investor B, because board presence and veto rights bite on actual decisions
They are equal, because both are minority shareholders
Neither, because the founders hold the rest
body.explanation: Investor A can block a special resolution and little else. Investor B sits in the room where decisions are made and can stop the company from borrowing, spending or selling itself. Real control follows the agreement, not just the cap table.

body.title: The term sheet on your desk
body.scenario: You are the finance lead at a Kochi-based logistics software company. The founders hold 100% of 20,00,000 shares. A fund offers ₹10 crore at a ₹40 crore pre-money valuation, with a 12% ESOP pool to be carved out of the pre-money, one board seat out of four, and consent rights over any new borrowing above ₹1 crore, the annual budget, and any sale of the company. The founders are delighted with the ₹50 crore post-money headline.
body.prompt: What would you flag to the founders before they sign?
body.modelAnswer:
On the numbers:
1. The ₹10 crore of ₹50 crore post-money is 20% to the fund. Add the 12% pool carved out of the pre-money and the founders are left with 68%, not 80%. The pool costs them 12 points, not 12 points shared with the investor.
2. Because the pool comes out of the pre-money, the effective pre-money valuation is lower than ₹40 crore. Ask what the number looks like with the pool created post-round, and negotiate the pool size against an actual hiring plan rather than a round 12%.
3. Model the next round too. Another 20% dilution takes the founders from 68% to about 54%, and the round after that takes them below half.

On control:
4. One seat of four is not a blocking position, but check who appoints the other three and whether the chair has a casting vote.
5. The consent right over borrowing above ₹1 crore is very tight for a logistics business that may need working capital limits. Negotiate the threshold up, or exclude ordinary course working capital facilities.
6. A consent right over the annual budget effectively gives the fund a say in hiring and spending all year. Ask for a deadlock resolution mechanism so a disagreement cannot freeze the company.
7. Ask how long these rights last: do they fall away if the fund's holding drops below a threshold, or at an IPO?

The headline valuation is the least negotiable-looking number on the page and often the least important one.

body.title: Before agreeing to any equity round
steps: Calculate the price per share yourself from the pre-money valuation and the existing share count
Confirm whether the ESOP pool is carved out of the pre-money or created after the round
Work out your stake after this round, and after one more round of similar size
List the reserved matters and ask what each one blocks in practice
Check the board composition after the round, not just the shareholding
Confirm the authorised share capital is high enough for the new shares
Ask when investor rights expire: on exit, at IPO, or below a holding threshold

cards.definition: What the company is agreed to be worth before the new money arrives. It sets the price per share.
Pre-money plus the amount raised. The investor's stake is their cheque divided by this.
The fall in an existing holder's percentage when new shares are issued. Their share count does not change.
Shares reserved for employee options. Whether it is carved out pre-money or post-round changes who pays for it.
More votes for than against, under Section 114(1) of the Companies Act, 2013.
Votes in favour at least three times votes against, effectively 75%, under Section 114(2).
Decisions requiring a named investor's consent, written into the shareholders' agreement.
Issuing shares to a specific investor under Section 62, needing a special resolution and a registered valuer report.

points: Equity is sold permanently. There is no repayment date and no way to buy the slice back except by negotiating with the holder.
Price per share comes from the pre-money valuation divided by the existing share count.
Dilution changes percentages, never the number of shares an existing holder owns.
An ESOP pool carved out of the pre-money is paid for entirely by the founders, which makes the headline valuation misleading.
Voting thresholds that matter in India: more than 50% to pass an ordinary resolution, 75% for a special resolution, more than 25% to block one.
Board seats and reserved matters give real control that no shareholding percentage reveals.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Meridian Learning and the other unnamed companies are fictional illustrations. Shareholding figures for real listed companies were accurate as reported on the dates mentioned and change every quarter.
